saa-ini-097.text: The financial team needs to know how much each project and each department spends on AWS, but all resources are mixed into the same account. What practice allows categorizing the costs per project in billing reports?
options: Create a user IAM per project
Print monthly invoice and divide manually into spreadsheets
Apply standardized tags (e.g. project, department) to resources and activate them as cost allocation tags in Billing
Rename instances with project name
saa-ini-097.explanation: Cost allocation tags, after being applied to the resources and activated on the billing console, become filter dimensions in the Cost Explorer and no CUR — enabling the view of expenditure by project and area.
saa-ini-097.hint: Label each resource with its 'gift' and notify the billing system to consider these labels.
optionRationales: Cost allocation tags, after being applied to the resources and activated on the billing console, become filter dimensions in the Cost Explorer and no CUR — enabling the view of expenditure by project and area.
The friendly name is not a structured billing dimension; without enabled allocation tags, reports do not group for this information.
The manual division is laborious, error-prone and unnecessary — the platform offers automatic categorization via tags.
Users IAM control ACESSO, non-attribution of costs — the person who creates the resource does not define the category of collection in the reports.

saa-ini-098.text: When reviewing the invoice, a company was surprised with the item 'Data Transfer'. About data transfer costs in AWS, what general rule the architect should consider when designing cost-optimized solutions?
options: Transfer costs exist only in the first year of the account
The data entry is the most expensive, to discourage migration
Any data transfer in the AWS is free, in any direction
Data entry (in) is usually free, while the exit to the internet (out) and traffic between AZs and Regions generate costs
saa-ini-098.explanation: The basic rule of transfer: data entering the AWS are not charged; the charge affects the exit to the internet and the traffic between AZs and between regions – therefore optimized architectures minimize these flows.
saa-ini-098.hint: Entering is free; leaving (and crossing internal borders) is what costs.
optionRationales: The basic rule of transfer: data entering the AWS are not charged; the charge affects the exit to the internet and the traffic between AZs and between regions – therefore optimized architectures minimize these flows.
The exit to the internet and traffic between AZs/Regions are charged — ignoring this generates surprises just like that of the scenario.
It's the opposite: entry is free just to facilitate cloud adoption.
Transfer costs are permanent and proportional to volume — there is no age exemption from the account.

saa-ini-099.text: A cost analysis identified dozens of volumes EBS 'orphans' (not attached to any instance), forgotten old snapshots and unused Elastic IPs. Why these resources deserve immediate attention in cost optimization?
options: Because they're a higher safety risk than the cost.
Because orphaned resources are automatically deleted by AWS, causing data loss
Because they continue to be charged in full even without generating any value, being the waste easier to eliminate
Because they prevent the creation of new resources in the account
saa-ini-099.explanation: Unattached volumes, accumulated snapshots and idle IPs continue on the bill month after month with no benefit — identifying and removing them is the fastest win of any optimization program.
saa-ini-099.hint: Think of where forgotten resources in the cloud continue to appear, month after month, even without generating any benefits.
optionRationales: Unattached volumes, accumulated snapshots and idle IPs continue on the bill month after month with no benefit — identifying and removing them is the fastest win of any optimization program.
A AWS does not exclude the customer's resources by idleness — they remain (and continue to be charged) until the customer acts.
Except for very specific quota limits, idle resources do not block new provisions — their problem is purely financial.
While resource hygiene also benefits safety, the central point of idle volumes/IPs in cost discipline is valueless continuous collection.

saa-ini-100.text: A company wants to quickly check if it is leaving money on the table: idle instances, unused volumes, loose IPs and opportunities for Reserved Instances. Which tool of the AWS already includes automatic cost optimization checks ready for use, with actionable recommendations?
options: AWS CloudFormation
AWS Trusted Advisor (cost optimization category)
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS X-Ray
saa-ini-100.explanation: The Trusted Advisor includes ready-to-cost checks — instances EC2 underutilized, volumes EBS orphans, idle IPs, use of reservations — with direct recommendations, without prior configuration.
saa-ini-100.hint: It is the 'trust counselor' who points waste without needing to set up anything.
optionRationales: The Trusted Advisor includes ready-to-cost checks — instances EC2 underutilized, volumes EBS orphans, idle IPs, use of reservations — with direct recommendations, without prior configuration.
The CloudFormation provides infrastructure as code — does not audit waste or recommends savings.
The GuardDuty detects security threats — does not analyze cost efficiency.
X-Ray tracks distributed requests for application performance debugging — is not cost optimization tool.

saa-ini-101.text: When a new order is created in an e-commerce system, three different systems need to be notified immediately: billing, stocking and sending confirmation emails. The architect wants to publish a single message that is automatically delivered to all these registered destinations, without the order system needing to know each of them. AWS meets this requirement?
options: Amazon SNS, which allows you to post a message in a topic and automatically deliver it to all subscribers (subscribers) registered
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, creating a stream that each system continuously consumes
AWS Step Functions, creating a workflow that calls each system in sequence
Amazon SQS, setting up a separate row for each of the three systems and sending the same message manually for each row
saa-ini-101.explanation: Correct. Amazon SNS implements the publishing/subscribe standard (fan-out): a single message published in a topic is automatically delivered to all registered subscribers, such as rows SQS, functions Lambda or e-mail.
saa-ini-101.hint: Think of the publication/signature service that automatically delivers a message to all destinations listed in a topic.
optionRationales: Correct. Amazon SNS implements the publishing/subscribe standard (fan-out): a single message published in a topic is automatically delivered to all registered subscribers, such as rows SQS, functions Lambda or e-mail.

The Amazon SQS is a point-to-point row: each message is usually consumed by a single recipient. Sending it manually to multiple rows would require extra logic in the ordering system, which the SNS resolve natively.
The Step Functions orchestrate workflows with sequential or parallel steps explicitly defined, but was not designed as a publication/signature mechanism to notify multiple uncoupled systems.

The Kinesis Data Streams is focused on ingesting and processing large volumes of real-time data (streaming) and requires management of shards and consumers — a more complex solution than is necessary for this reporting scenario.

saa-ini-102.text: An instance EC2 performing a critical workload (without being part of a Auto Scaling Group) occasionally becomes unavailable due to hardware failures of the underlying physical host. The architect wants the AWS automatically detect this hardware failure and retrieve the instance — preserving the same ID, private IP address, metadata and data in the volumes EBS — without manual intervention. What it should set up?
options: Associate the instance to a Network Load Balancer with health checks configured
Place the instance in a Auto Scaling Group with minimum and desired capacity equal to 1
Migrate the instance to a type (type instance) with more vCPUs and memory
An alarm from the Amazon CloudWatch based on the StatusCheckFailed_System metric, with the action of automatically recovering the instance ("recover")
saa-ini-102.explanation: Correct. CloudWatch in the system status check metric (which detects problems in the underlying hardware/host), configured with the 'recover' action, automatically migrates the instance to a new hardware, preserving ID, private IP, metadata and data in EBS.
saa-ini-102.hint: Think about the resource of CloudWatch which can automatically trigger a recovery action from the instance itself when detecting failure in the underlying hardware.
optionRationales: Correct. CloudWatch in the system status check metric (which detects problems in the underlying hardware/host), configured with the 'recover' action, automatically migrates the instance to a new hardware, preserving ID, private IP, metadata and data in EBS.

One Auto Scaling Group would replace the default instance by a new instance — with a new ID and, in general, a new private IP — which does not meet the requirement to preserve the same instance and its identifiers.
A Network Load Balancer just stop sending traffic to an unhealthy target; it does not recover or replace the instance with hardware failure.
Increasing the size of the instance does not prevent or resolve hardware failures in the underlying physical host — the problem is not related to the instance processing capacity.

saa-ini-103.text: A team set up automatic backups on Amazon RDS with a retention period of 7 days. A failure in an implementation corrupted important data to 14Yesterday's h32. The team needs to restore the database exactly to the state in which it was a few minutes before the corruption, without losing the transactions that occurred before that time. Amazon RDS allows this restoration?
options: Point-in-time restoration (PITR), creating a new database instance with data in the state of a specific moment within the backup retention period
Perform the failover of a Multi-AZ deployment for standby
Promote an existing Read Replica to the main instance
Restore the manual snapshot created at the time the database was originally created
saa-ini-103.explanation: Right. The point-in-time restoration of the RDS combines the automatic daily snapshot with transaction logs, allowing to recreate the bank in a new instance in the exact state of any second within the configured retention period.
saa-ini-103.hint: Think of the feature that combines daily backups with transaction logs to restore the database to any second within the set retention period.
optionRationales: Right. The point-in-time restoration of the RDS combines the automatic daily snapshot with transaction logs, allowing to recreate the bank in a new instance in the exact state of any second within the configured retention period.
A Read Replica is continuously updated with the same changes from the main instance — including data corruption — and does not offer a mechanism to 'return in time' until an earlier moment.
In a Multi-AZ deployment, the standby is maintained synchronized by synchronous replication; data corruption would also be replicated to the standby, so the failover does not solve the problem.

A snapshot of the moment of creation reflects only the initial state of the bank, without any of the legitimate transactions occurring later — restoring it would cause much greater loss of data than punctual corruption..

saa-ini-104.text: An application uses one Application Load Balancer with instances EC2 unequally recorded between two Availability Zones: 6 fora AZ-A and 2 fora AZ-B. The team realizes that, without any additional configuration, traffic is distributed so that each instance — regardless of AZ — receives approximately the same amount of requests. Application Load Balancer, enabled by default, explains this behavior?
options: Cross-area balancing, which distributes traffic uniformly among all registered targets, regardless of the Availability Zone in which they are located
Persistent sessions (sticky sessions), which keep each user always in the same instance
Health checks, which remove unhealthy instances from rotation
Connection draining (deregistration delay), which allows connections in progress to end before removing an instance
saa-ini-104.explanation: Correct. Application Load Balancer, the balancing between zones is enabled by default and cannot be disabled: the total traffic is equally distributed among all registered instances, not only equally divided between the AZs and the AZs..
saa-ini-104.hint: Think about the configuration of Application Load Balancer, active by default and which cannot be disconnected, which distributes requests equally among all target instances, not only between Availability Zones.
optionRationales: Correct. Application Load Balancer, the balancing between zones is enabled by default and cannot be disabled: the total traffic is equally distributed among all registered instances, not only equally divided between the AZs and the AZs..
Persistent sessions control which instance the requests of the same user are directed to, but do not explain why the total load is balanced by instance between AZs with different number of instances.
Health checks only determine whether an instance may or may not receive traffic; they do not balance the amount of requests per instance between different Availability Zones.
Connection drainage deals with the graceful removal of balancing instances, but is not the resource responsible for distributing traffic evenly between instances in different AZs.

saa-ini-105.text: A company wants to gradually launch a new version of its application, hosted on a separate set of servers. Initially, only 10% of production traffic should be directed to the new version, with the others 90% continue in the current version. The proportion can be adjusted over the next days. Amazon Route 53 allows traffic to be distributed in this way?
options: Geographical route (geolocation routing), which directs traffic based on user location
Failover routing, which directs all traffic to a secondary resource if the primary is unavailable
Latency-based routing (latency-based routing), which directs the user to the region with lower latency
Weighted routing, which distributes requests across multiple resources according to the weights defined by the administrator
saa-ini-105.explanation: Correct. The weighted routing of Route 53 allows to assign a relative weight to each record, controlling the proportion of traffic directed to each resource — ideal for gradual releases (canary releases)).
saa-ini-105.hint: Think about the policy of routing the Route 53 allowing traffic to be divided between two resources according to a ratio manually defined by the administrator.
optionRationales: Correct. The weighted routing of Route 53 allows to assign a relative weight to each record, controlling the proportion of traffic directed to each resource — ideal for gradual releases (canary releases)).

Failover routing is all-or-nothing: it directs 100% from traffic to the main resource while it is healthy, and only changes to secondary in case of failure — does not allow sharing traffic in fixed percentages.
Latency-based routing automatically chooses the lowest perceived latency feature for each user, but does not offer direct control over a percentage ratio defined by the administrator.
Geographical router directs users to specific resources based on their geographical location, not based on a configurable percentage proportion independent of location.

saa-ini-107.text: A table of the Amazon DynamoDB store critical data from a financial application. By compliance requirement, the company needs to be able to restore the table to any point in time within the last 35 days, in case of exclusion or accidental recording of items. DynamoDB must be enabled to meet this requirement?
options: DynamoDB Streams
Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)
Global Tables
Auto Scaling of the DynamoDB
saa-ini-107.explanation: The Point-in-Time Recovery of DynamoDB, when enabled, it allows to restore the table for any second within a window held from up to 35 days, protecting against accidental exclusions or recordings.
saa-ini-107.hint: Think about the resource of DynamoDB which allows to restore the table for any second inside a window held from up 35 days.
optionRationales: The Point-in-Time Recovery of DynamoDB, when enabled, it allows to restore the table for any second within a window held from up to 35 days, protecting against accidental exclusions or recordings.

The DynamoDB Streams captures an orderly record of changes to items for external applications (as functions Lambda) process these changes — it is not in itself a mechanism for restoring the table to a point in time.
Global Tables replicate the table among multiple Regions for high availability and low global latency, but do not offer a restoration mechanism for a point in the previous time.
The Auto Scaling of the DynamoDB automatically adjusts the read/write capability based on demand — has no relation to backup or data restoration.

saa-ini-108.text: A request processing system receives sudden and unpredictable traffic peaks. During these peaks, the service responsible for processing the requests — which runs in a fixed number of instances — becomes overloaded and begins to reject new requests. The architect wants to unplug the receipt of requests for their processing, so that no request is lost during the peaks, even if processing takes longer to clear the accumulated demand.?
options: Manually increase the size of processing instances whenever a traffic peak is perceived
Insert a row of the Amazon SQS between the receipt and processing of requests, allowing the processing service to consume messages at its own pace
Reduce timeout of requests HTTP received by the system of applications
Configure the Auto Scaling processing service to reduce the number of instances during peak traffic
saa-ini-108.explanation: Right. Amazon SQS uncouple consumer producers: it absorbs peak incoming messages and allows the processing service to consume at its own pace without losing orders during peak traffic.
saa-ini-108.hint: Think of the queue service that can receive high-speed messages during peaks and allow consumers to process them at their own pace.
optionRationales: Right. Amazon SQS uncouple consumer producers: it absorbs peak incoming messages and allows the processing service to consume at its own pace without losing orders during peak traffic.

Sudden and unpredictable peaks do not give sufficient time for manual intervention; moreover, resizing instances manually does not decouple the receipt of processing or avoid loss of requests during peak.
Reducing timeout makes requests fail faster during overload, but does not prevent requests from being rejected — actually, it would make the experience worse by discarding orders even faster.
Reducing capacity during a peak demand is the opposite of what the scenario needs — this would increase the burden and the rate of rejected applications.

saa-ini-109.text: A company needs to ensure that snapshots of volumes EBS of its bodies EC2 are automatically created every day, at a specified time, and that snapshots with more than 30 days are automatically excluded — without anyone having to perform this process manually. AWS meets this need?
options: Manually Create One AMI of the instance once a month
Use AWS Trusted Advisor to create snapshots daily
Enable 'version' directly in the volumes EBS by the console of the EC2
Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM), automating the creation, retention and deletion of volume snapshots EBS based on scheduled policies
saa-ini-109.explanation: Correct. Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager lets you define policies that create volume snapshots EBS automatically on a defined schedule and exclude older snapshots than a set retention period, without manual intervention.
saa-ini-109.hint: Think of the resource of AWS dedicated specifically to automating policies for creating and retaining volume snapshots EBS.
optionRationales: Correct. Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager lets you define policies that create volume snapshots EBS automatically on a defined schedule and exclude older snapshots than a set retention period, without manual intervention.
Volumes EBS they do not have a 'version' feature; this concept exists for objects of the Amazon S3, not for block volumes of EBS.
Create a AMI monthly does not meet the requirement for automated daily snapshots with automatic deletion after 30 days, in addition to continuing to depend on manual execution.
The AWS Trusted Advisor provides recommendations on cost, security, performance and other aspects of the account — it does not create or schedule volume snapshots EBS.
